blindSummary:
This region operates under a 2014 special-autonomy religious criminal code that criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women with penalties of up to 100 lashes or eight years' imprisonment — nothing like it exists in any other region of the country. Enforcement by the religious police and the regional order-enforcement agency is active and escalating: in February 2025 two men caught in a boarding house received a combined 159 lashes publicly in the region's main city for consensual sex (one collapsed at the end), and in August 2025 two men received 80 lashes each for hugging and kissing, with the net widening beyond sex to non-sexual contact. A boarding-house raid in February 2025 specifically detained a transfeminine person alongside a gay university student, and in January 2018 police detained and forcibly shaved twelve trans women.

The code does not name trans women explicitly, but the February 2025 raid shows enforcement reaches them, and no other region in the country carries an active corporal-punishment regime for consensual adult conduct. Risk here is state-imposed and judicially formalised: religious district courts hand down caning sentences carried out publicly on a stage in a city park before crowds, sometimes with the trial itself behind closed doors, for behaviour that is lawful elsewhere in the country.
blindSourceSummaries: A law-and-culture journal study (2025) on the growth of visible trans women in this region between social challenge and law enforcement: empirical-legal study of how the 2014 religious criminal code's offence categories (same-sex acts between men, between women, and cohabitation) are enforced against trans women, confirming that this region's special religious-law authority includes public caning applied where a violation occurs and that enforcement pressure falls on visible gender nonconformity.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time; the underlying international cable-news report (27 Feb 2025) covers two men publicly caned a combined 159 strokes in this region's main city after being caught by residents in a boarding house; one collapsed at the end of the punishment and was carried off by the religious police.

An international broadcaster and wire-service report (26 Aug 2025): two men aged 20 and 21 were publicly caned 80 strokes each in this region's main city, in a city park, after a religious district court convicted them of hugging and kissing (ruled as leading to banned sexual relations), before ~100 spectators, with eight more people caned the same day; notes this region permits up to 100 lashes for morality offences (gay sex, unmarried sex, gambling, drinking, women's 'tight' clothing) and that the trial itself was held behind closed doors; an international rights organisation called it 'state-sanctioned discrimination and cruelty'.

A local media report (18 Feb 2025): the main city's order-enforcement agency and religious police detained a pair — a transfeminine person and a gay university student — in a boarding-house room; the religious-police enforcement-division head confirmed they face up to 100 caning strokes under the religious code's same-sex conduct provision and urged guesthouse owners to police tenants, showing boarding-house round-ups on this basis are recurring and that trans women are swept up in enforcement.

A foreign university's human-rights institute commentary: trans women are the most frequent victims of police violence in the country's anti-LGBT upturn; records the January 2018 case where this region's police detained twelve trans women and forcibly shaved or cut their hair to teach them 'how to act like real men', within a national pattern of state failure to protect trans citizens.
